lines.text: October first, nineteen forty-eight. Second Lieutenant George Gorman, twenty-five, a wartime fighter pilot, flies a Mustang over Fargo, North Dakota. For the next twenty-seven minutes, he says, a light fights him in the dark.
The Air Force would call it a balloon. Gorman never agreed. He called it a dogfight, and in his statement he wrote that its moves showed, quote, a definite thought behind its maneuvers.
So tonight, we fly the circuit. Every airfield has one, a pattern of laps in the sky. We take the dogfight one leg at a time, from downwind to the final stall.
At each leg, we ask what is evidence, and what is rumor. Then we put the suspects on trial: a lighted balloon, the planet Jupiter, and a craft nobody built.
At the end, a verdict. Let's join the pattern, at nine o'clock on a Friday night.

Friday, October first. Hector Airport, Fargo. The North Dakota Air National Guard's squadron has flown in from a cross-country trip, and the other pilots have landed. Gorman stays up, to log some night flying time.
The sky is clear. He circles the lighted football stadium, a bright landmark in the dark, before turning for the field. Around nine o'clock, the tower clears him to land.

He checks the traffic with the tower. The controllers work for the Civil Aeronautics Administration. They say the only other aircraft up is a Piper Cub. Gorman can see it, about five hundred feet below him.
Remember that Cub. Its pilot and his passenger are about to become two of the witnesses.
Then, on his right, a light passes. Gorman takes it for the taillight of another plane. He asks the tower. The tower knows of no other aircraft.
He turns toward it. As he closes in, he sees what it is. A light, clear white, perfectly round, with sharp edges, and no fuzz. By his estimate, six to eight inches across at about a thousand yards.
It is blinking on and off. Then, as he gets closer, the blinking stops. The light goes steady, and it banks sharply to the left.
Gorman is a fighter pilot. He does what a fighter pilot does. He decides to catch it.
He pushes the throttle forward and dives, sixty inches of manifold pressure, all the Mustang has. He cannot close the distance. The light climbs away, and banks left again.
He tries to cut it off, to turn inside its path and meet it on the far side. He cannot. Each time, the light is somewhere else.
In the tower, controllers Lloyd Jensen and H. E. Johnson look up. They see a fast light, and the Mustang beside it. Quote, a round light, perfectly formed, no fuzzy edges.
And they see the gap grow. The light increases its spacing from the fighter. It is not drifting. It is leaving.

The Cub's pilot, Dr. A. E. Cannon, and his passenger, Einar Nielson, also see it. The swift light passes above them, much faster, they say, than the fifty-one. They land and watch from the tower with binoculars.
So beyond Gorman, there are four civilian witnesses. Two more Civil Aeronautics employees report seeing it as well. Six witnesses besides the pilot, in the air and on the ground.
No sound. No smell. No exhaust. And no change on any instrument in the cockpit. Gorman reports all of it afterward.
He puts the light's speed at up to four hundred miles an hour. That is fast, but not impossible in nineteen forty-eight. It is the turning that bothers him. Hold that thought.
Now the pattern tightens. Next leg: final approach, and the moment the light stops running away.
At about seven thousand feet, the chase changes. The light that has been running from him turns right, and comes straight at him. Head-on.
Gorman does what any pilot would. He dives to avoid it. The light passes over his canopy, about five hundred feet above him, by his judgement.
He circles left. The light is now about a thousand feet above. He lines up on it again.
In one of these hard turns, Gorman blacks out for a moment. Remember that when we weigh his account. A pilot who loses consciousness in a turn is not at his sharpest.
A second head-on pass. This time the light does not slide away sideways. It shoots straight up.
Gorman follows it into the climb. At about fourteen thousand feet, the Mustang stalls. The light keeps going.
Nine twenty-seven p.m. Gorman loses sight of it. By the clock, the encounter has lasted twenty-seven minutes.
He lands, and reports. His statement goes to Major D. C. Jones. The whole thing is on paper before he goes to bed.
In it, he says the moves showed, quote, a definite thought behind its maneuvers. But he also says the light was, quote, governed by the laws of inertia. Keep that second line in mind.
Within days, the Air Force's first UFO study, Project Sign, takes the case. Gorman's plane is checked, and a Geiger counter is run over it. It reads higher than normal.
Radioactive? No. The reading is later explained as cosmic rays, picked up during time at high altitude. Pilots do pick up a little.
The investigators judge the man. Quote, he did not make the impression of being a dreamer. A sincere and serious individual who was considerably puzzled.

He is no fantasist. A wartime fighter pilot. A construction company manager by day. A Guard officer at night. He will retire as a lieutenant colonel in nineteen sixty-nine, and die in nineteen eighty-two.
Edward Ruppelt, who later ran the Air Force's UFO project, calls it one of the three classics of nineteen forty-eight. The others are the Mantell crash, and the Chiles-Whitted airliner sighting.
Look at what is missing. No photograph. No wreckage. No physical trace on the ground. What we have is testimony.
But it is a lot of testimony. A pilot in the air, controllers in the tower, a doctor and his passenger in a small plane. All of them saw a fast, round light that night. Something was there.
So what was it? The Air Force had an answer ready. And it was only ten minutes old.
The official explanation is a lighted weather balloon. The Air Weather Service released one from Fargo at about eight-fifty that evening. That is roughly ten minutes before Gorman's first sighting.
A small balloon with a lamp drifts with the wind. At night, with no horizon and no sense of size, it looks like a steady point of light.
The early reviews add another suspect. Jupiter was bright in the sky that night. Project Sign and Project Grudge point to Jupiter and a balloon together.
Astronomer Donald Menzel later argues for a balloon, plus a mirage of Jupiter. The final Blue Book label is simply: lighted balloon.
Ruppelt gives a reason why the passes look so strange. When a fast plane overtakes a slow balloon, he explains, it can look like the object is rushing past head-on. The turns are all yours.
Decades later, Dr. James McDonald reads the Blue Book file itself, in nineteen seventy. He finds explicit statements in it that discount the balloon.
And Gorman himself never accepted it. He told friends he was never convinced he had spent twenty-seven minutes dueling with a balloon. So let's put the balloon on trial.
Suspect one: the lighted weather balloon. The official answer. The one that sits on the paperwork.
Here is what favors it. A lighted balloon really was released from Fargo. The timing fits. And it is a small, round point of light, much like what he describes.
Night flying is also a trap for the eyes. No horizon. No landmarks. A single light, with nothing to measure it against. Distance and speed are close to impossible to judge.
Now what counts against it. Gorman followed the light for twenty-seven minutes, through dives, climbs and turns. A balloon drifts with the wind. It does not seem to turn away from a fighter.
The controllers said the light increased its spacing from the Mustang. The pilot said it ran from him at up to four hundred miles an hour. A balloon cannot outrun an F-51.
Ruppelt's illusion is clever, and it can explain the head-on passes. But it asks us to believe the passes were Gorman's own turns, and that he and six others misjudged the speeds.
And McDonald's finding matters here. The very file that carries the balloon label also carries statements that discount it. The label is official. The reasoning is thin.
So the balloon is real, and possibly part of the story. But it does not cleanly explain the speed. That leaves another suspect, and some stranger ones.
Suspect two: Jupiter, and the others. Jupiter really was in the sky that night, bright and low. Sign and Grudge both pointed to it.
Menzel argued a mirage could make Jupiter jump, and flicker, and seem to move. A mirage can change a light's position. It does not fly past a pilot's canopy.
Gorman flew at night for years. He knew a planet. Jupiter does not blink on and off, bank sharply, and shoot straight up. This one is a weak fit.
A third idea comes from the Cold War. A Soviet rocket test. Aerospace engineer Travis Taylor looks at it and rejects it. The range is wrong, and rockets of that era could not maneuver.

That leaves the last suspect: a craft that nobody built, an intelligence flying with, quote, a definite thought. It would explain the maneuvers. It has no hardware, no photograph, and no second witness who could say what it was.
Time to score the case. Not what we hope. What the file supports.
Debrief. Time to score the Gorman case.

A real flight and a real report: evidence. Six witnesses besides Gorman saw a fast, round light: evidence. A balloon was released ten minutes before: evidence. A balloon alone, fitting the speed: unlikely. A mirage of Jupiter: unlikely.
A radioactive craft: debunked, it was cosmic rays. A Soviet rocket: debunked. A craft from elsewhere: no evidence at all.
The verdict. The sighting was real, and the witnesses were credible. A balloon is the best candidate, but it leaves the speed unexplained. Open case, narrowing but not closed.
The strangest part is how ordinary it was. A pilot with time to spare, a clear Friday night, and a light that would not let him go. He never accepted the balloon answer.
Next case: a farmhouse in Kentucky, nineteen fifty-five, a family, and little men at the window. A siege that lasted all night. Was it real?
What do you think Gorman saw? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
